newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S., Russia may ratify chemical weapons pact soon.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Russia may ratify chemical weapons pact soon.

text.p: The United States and Russia may still ratify the landmark Chemical Weapons Convention before its entry into force on April 29, the executive secretary of the Hague-based commission overseeing the accord said on Monday.

The world's two largest possessors of chemical weapons -- with declared stocks of some 70,000 tonnes between them -- have both signed the treaty prohibiting the development, production or use of chemical weapons, but both have yet to ratify it.

"In the U.S., the administration assures us that now the election is over the President intends to press for an early ratification -- so we are fairly hopeful," Ian Kenyon, executive secretary of the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) told a news conference.
"And in the Russian Republic, the Duma recently passed a law requiring the destruction of all stocks of chemical weapons, so we hope to see ratification there fairly shortly, too."

The U.S. Senate was to have voted on ratification in September last year but the issue was set aside amid assessments it would be hamstrung with unacceptable amendments or defeated after coming under fire from conservatives during the U.S. presidential election campaign.
"When the senators look at the matter away from the context of the election they will realise the concept...is too important to be used as a political football," Kenyon said.

The chemical weapons convention has been signed by 160 states and been ratified by 67 of those so far. Its entry into force was triggered on October 31, when Hungary became the 65th state to ratify the pact.
The inaugural conference of the OPCW will be held in the Hague on May 6, Kenyon said, with nations which have not yet ratified the convention unable to vote.
"The first conference will be very important. It will take a lot of decisions about the organisation itself." Kenyon said.
"The U.S. administration is well aware of how important it is and they have told me they intend to do all they can to get there."

The pact -- the first multilateral agreement to eliminate a whole category of weapons -- contains tough verification measures and the OPCW has already begun training inspectors from 56 countries to carry out the task.
Signatories must destroy all their chemical weapons within 10 years and provide detailed information about the production and export of listed chemicals used to make such weapons.
They are barred from supplying listed chemicals to non-signatories and must open their chemical plants to the OPCW both for routine and short-notice inspections.
If an inspection confirms a violation, the offending state faces expulsion from the OPCW and possibly even United Nations sanctions.
Around 150 experts have accepted offers to join the first training group, the OPCW said, including munitions specialists, analytical and industrial chemists and chemical production logisticians.
